sections.section_title: The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis

focus_areas: Iron law of ML performance and Amdahl speedup limits
Physics of GPU memory hierarchy and access energy ladder
Generational shifts in roofline ridge points from V100 to B200
Arithmetic intensity classification of ML workloads (GEMM, GELU, LLM decode)
rationale.question_strategy: Begin with an iron law decomposition calculation, follow with generational ridge point analysis, test memory hierarchy physics with an ordering and an energy scenario, and clarify arithmetic intensity as an algorithmic property.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Amdahl math application -> generational system reasoning -> memory hierarchy ordering -> conceptual definition check -> thermodynamic energy evaluation.
rationale.integration: Connects foundational hardware acceleration and memory hierarchy concepts from earlier chapters to the performance engineering diagnostic equation.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Foundational section establishing the governing performance equation, memory wall physics, and roofline diagnosis.

questions.question: A training step's wall-clock time is decomposed via the iron law of ML performance ($T = D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}$) into 60% memory traffic ($D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$), 30% compute execution ($O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}})$), and 10% dispatch and latency overhead ($L_{\text{lat}}$). A hardware upgrade doubles the GPU's peak dense FP16 compute ($R_{\text{peak}}$) while leaving memory bandwidth ($\text{BW}$) and software latency ($L_{\text{lat}}$) unchanged. What is the maximum theoretical speedup this upgrade can achieve on this workload?
choices: Approximately $1.18\times$ speedup (a 15% reduction in step time), because doubling compute only reduces the 30% compute slice to 15% while the 70% non-compute time remains unchanged
$2.00\times$ speedup, because doubling peak compute throughput halves the overall execution time of matrix multiplication operations
$1.67\times$ speedup, because the 30% compute fraction and 10% latency fraction are both accelerated by the faster clock frequency
$1.43\times$ speedup, because the memory-bound portion is compressed by the faster arithmetic execution units
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Approximately $1.18\times$ speedup (a 15% reduction in step time), because doubling compute only reduces the 30% compute slice to 15% while the 70% non-compute time remains unchanged. Under the iron law ($T = D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}$), doubling $R_{\text{peak}}$ only affects the compute term, halving it from 0.30 to 0.15 of the baseline time. The new normalized time is $0.60 + 0.15 + 0.10 = 0.85$, yielding a speedup of $1.0 / 0.85 \approx 1.18\times$. Expecting a $2.0\times$ speedup commits the classic Amdahl's law fallacy by ignoring that 70% of execution is governed by memory bandwidth and latency, while the other choices incorrectly assume compute hardware improvements accelerate memory transfers or fixed software dispatch overhead.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the iron law of ML performance to calculate the theoretical speedup of targeted hardware upgrades under Amdahl's law constraints

questions.question: An operation has an arithmetic intensity of 200 FLOP/byte. On an NVIDIA V100 (ridge point $\approx 139\text{ FLOP/byte}$) and an H100 (ridge point $\approx 295\text{ FLOP/byte}$), how does the workload's operational bottleneck shift across generations, and what is the primary systems implication for performance optimization?
questions.answer: The operation shifts from being compute-bound on the V100 (since $200 > 139$) to memory-bound on the H100 (since $200 < 295$). The systems implication is that compute optimizations (such as improving instruction scheduling) are sufficient on V100, but memory-reduction techniques (such as operator fusion, tiling, and precision quantization) become mandatory on H100 to achieve higher throughput because compute throughput grew ($7.9\times$) much faster than memory bandwidth ($3.7\times$).
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how generational shifts in hardware balance points change the active performance bottleneck of ML workloads

questions.question: Order the following levels of the GPU memory hierarchy from nearest to the streaming multiprocessor arithmetic units to farthest: (1) L2 Cache, (2) Registers, (3) High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), (4) Shared Memory (SRAM).
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) Registers -> (4) Shared Memory (SRAM) -> (1) L2 Cache -> (3) High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Registers and shared memory provide local working storage, L2 serves reuse across SMs, and off-chip HBM supplies bulk capacity. Keeping reusable intermediates near compute avoids costly off-chip transfers; numerical energy comparisons additionally require a common transaction size and measurement boundary.
questions.learning_objective: Order GPU storage tiers by proximity to compute and explain the cost of off-chip traffic.

questions.question: True or False: Arithmetic intensity is a fixed, intrinsic property of a neural network architecture that remains invariant regardless of batch size or kernel implementation choices.
questions.answer: False. Arithmetic intensity ($I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{bytes}$) is an algorithmic and implementation-dependent property, not an invariant model constant. For instance, increasing the serving batch size amortizes model weight loading across more requests, raising arithmetic intensity linearly with batch size, while operator fusion increases arithmetic intensity by keeping intermediate activations in on-chip SRAM instead of round-tripping through HBM.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the relationship between workload arithmetic intensity, implementation strategies, and batch dimensions

questions.question: What is the primary energy and performance consequence of repeatedly streaming intermediate tensors through off-chip HBM rather than retaining them in on-chip SRAM?
choices: Off-chip transfers bypass the L2 cache entirely, preventing the GPU memory management unit from performing virtual address translation
Off-chip transfers consume memory-interface energy and can limit throughput through bandwidth and latency, whereas retaining reusable intermediates in SRAM reduces HBM traffic
Streaming through HBM causes numerical drift and precision loss because DRAM capacitors lose charge over multi-nanosecond round-trips
SRAM access draws higher total power because operating at higher clock frequencies increases dynamic capacitance dissipation beyond HBM interface PHYs
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Repeated off-chip transfers consume energy and bandwidth without adding useful arithmetic. Fusion and tiling can retain intermediates in SRAM and reduce that traffic, subject to local capacity and occupancy constraints. Neither numerical precision drift in DRAM nor failed address translation explains this bottleneck; transaction-size conventions are needed before comparing access energies quantitatively.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the thermodynamic and latency consequences of off-chip HBM data movement versus on-chip SRAM caching

sections.section_title: Serving Regimes, Batch Size, and Prefill-Decode

focus_areas: Arithmetic intensity scaling with batch size
Prefill compute-bound vs decode memory-bound characteristics
PagedAttention eliminating internal KV cache fragmentation
Roofline analysis of 70B LLM decode on H100 clusters
rationale.question_strategy: Contrast the computational profiles of prefill and decode in an MCQ, probe PagedAttention memory mechanics in a SHORT question, test disaggregated serving terminology in a FILL question, and compute bandwidth-bound decode limits in a multi-GPU scenario MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Phase classification -> memory fragmentation mechanics -> terminology recall -> quantitative roofline decode calculation.
rationale.integration: Bridges single-node roofline physics to serving systems, showing how batch dimensions and phase separation alter operational bottlenecks.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Key serving architecture section establishing the trade-offs of batching and the prefill-decode split.

questions.question: In modern Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems, why do the prompt prefill phase and the token decode phase exhibit fundamentally different performance bottlenecks on GPU hardware?
choices: Prefill generates tokens sequentially one by one, making it memory-bound by weight reads, whereas decode processes all prompt tokens in parallel, making it compute-bound by Tensor Cores
Prefill relies exclusively on integer arithmetic units, whereas decode requires floating-point matrix multiplication units

Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel via large GEMMs, achieving high arithmetic intensity and compute-bound Tensor Core execution, whereas single-request decode reads all model weights to generate a single token, operating deep in the memory-bound regime
Prefill requires continuous network AllToAll collective exchanges between GPUs, whereas decode requires no inter-GPU communication
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel via large GEMMs, achieving high arithmetic intensity and compute-bound Tensor Core execution, whereas single-request decode reads all model weights to generate a single token, operating deep in the memory-bound regime. For a prompt of $S=1024$ tokens, prefill executes a matrix multiplication of shape $[S, d_{\text{model}}] \times [d_{\text{model}}, d_{\text{model}}]$, achieving an arithmetic intensity of $\sim 1024\text{ FLOP/byte}$ for FP16 weights, which saturates Tensor Cores. In contrast, batch-1 autoregressive decode reads the entire weight tensor to compute a single output token, giving an arithmetic intensity of $\sim 1\text{ FLOP/byte}$, which leaves Tensor Cores mostly idle while waiting for HBM bandwidth. The other choices invert the phases, falsely claim differing arithmetic types, or fabricate communication differences.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the computational characteristics and primary hardware bottlenecks of the prefill and decode serving phases

questions.question: Explain how PagedAttention enables a 2–4$\times$ throughput improvement in LLM serving without modifying model weights or numerical precision, contrasting its memory allocation mechanism with traditional contiguous preallocation.
questions.answer: Contiguous preallocation reserves capacity for each request's maximum length, leaving unused slots when sequences are shorter. PagedAttention allocates fixed-size blocks as sequences grow and reuses free blocks across requests, sharply reducing allocation waste, though a final partly filled block can remain. The recovered capacity permits larger batches; reported 2–4-fold throughput gains depend on the workload and latency constraint rather than following automatically from paging.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how paged allocation reduces KV fragmentation and can expand batch capacity.

questions.question: The architectural pattern that decouples LLM inference by executing the compute-bound prompt prefill phase and the bandwidth-bound autoregressive token decode phase on separate, specialized hardware pools is known as ____ serving.
questions.answer: disaggregated. Separate pools specialize for prompt processing and token generation; transferring the KV cache between them adds a communication cost that the specialization must repay.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the architectural term for separating prefill and decode workloads across specialized hardware pools

questions.question: A 70B parameter LLM (140 GB FP16 weights) is served across an 8-GPU NVIDIA H100 node with tensor parallelism (TP=8). Each GPU holds 17.5 GB of weights and provides 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth and 989 TFLOP/s peak FP16 compute. At batch size 1, what is the theoretical bandwidth-limited decode step time per token, and why is achieved compute utilization below 0.4%?
choices: Decode takes approximately 120 ms per token because NVLink latency serializes the 8 GPUs, consuming 99.6% of time in network barriers
Decode takes approximately 0.5 ms per token because the 8 GPUs execute in parallel at peak FP16 compute throughput
Decode takes approximately 24.0 ms per token because the GPU must reread the entire 140 GB model across the PCI-e bus on each step

Decode takes approximately 5.2 ms per token ($17.5\text{ GB} / 3.35\text{ TB/s}$), and compute utilization is below 0.4% because the arithmetic intensity is only 1.0 FLOP/byte compared to the H100 ridge point of ~295 FLOP/byte
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Decode takes approximately 5.2 ms per token ($17.5\text{ GB} / 3.35\text{ TB/s}$), and compute utilization is below 0.4% because the arithmetic intensity is only 1.0 FLOP/byte compared to the H100 ridge point of ~295 FLOP/byte. At batch size 1 with TP=8, each GPU reads its 17.5 GB weight shard once per token: $T_{\text{decode}} = 17.5\text{ GB} / 3.35\text{ TB/s} \approx 5.2\text{ ms}$. Each GPU executes $2 \times 8.75 \times 10^9 = 1.75 \times 10^{10}\text{ FLOP}$, giving an arithmetic intensity of $\frac{1.75 \times 10^{10}\text{ FLOP}}{1.75 \times 10^{10}\text{ bytes}} = 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$. The achieved compute rate is $1.75 \times 10^{10} / 0.00522 \approx 3.35\text{ TFLOP/s}$, which is only $3.35 / 989 \approx 0.34\%$ of the H100's peak compute. The other options miscalculate memory transfer times, confuse single-GPU shards with full model weights, or postulate unrealistic PCIe and NVLink stalls.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the theoretical decode step time and hardware utilization of a tensor-parallel LLM deployment using roofline principles

focus_areas: Intermediate HBM traffic reduction from fusion
Categories of fusion (element-wise, reduction, operator-specific)
CUDA Graphs eliminating CPU launch latency and determinism constraints
FlashAttention online softmax tiling and algorithmic FLOP trade-offs
rationale.question_strategy: Order the steps of online softmax, examine CUDA Graph execution constraints, probe FlashAttention's I/O-aware FLOP vs memory trade-off, clarify CUDA Graph fusion misconceptions, and evaluate HBM traffic savings in an operator fusion chain.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Algorithmic step ordering -> runtime constraint evaluation -> deep systems trade-off analysis -> mechanism distinction -> quantitative traffic calculation.
rationale.integration: Demonstrates how kernel engineering and compiler techniques operationalize memory hierarchy principles to defeat the memory wall.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core kernel engineering section covering the primary techniques for reclaiming bandwidth and dispatch overhead.

questions.question:
In FlashAttention's online softmax algorithm, arrange the following steps in the exact order executed when processing tile $t$ of key-value blocks in fast on-chip SRAM:

(1) Rescale previous running sum and output accumulator by multiplying by $e^{m_{\text{old}} - m_{\text{new}}}$
(2) Compute local block of attention scores $A_t = Q_{\text{block}} K_t^T$
(3) Compute local softmax probabilities with $m_{\text{new}}$ and accumulate into running output
(4) Update the running maximum: $m_{\text{new}} = \max(m_{\text{old}}, \max(A_t))$
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) Compute local block of attention scores $A_t = Q_{\text{block}} K_t^T$ -> (4) Update the running maximum: $m_{\text{new}} = \max(m_{\text{old}}, \max(A_t))$ -> (1) Rescale previous running sum and output accumulator by multiplying by $e^{m_{\text{old}} - m_{\text{new}}}$ -> (3) Compute local softmax probabilities with $m_{\text{new}}$ and accumulate into running output. The algorithm first computes the local tile scores, updates the running maximum to incorporate the new tile's peak, rescales previous partial accumulators using the difference between old and new maxima, and finally accumulates the new tile's softmax contribution.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the algorithmic sequence of online softmax tiling in FlashAttention to maintain numerical exactness in on-chip SRAM

questions.question: Why are CUDA Graphs highly effective at accelerating the autoregressive decode phase of Large Language Models, but significantly more difficult to apply to the prompt prefill phase?
choices: CUDA Graphs require deterministic execution with fixed tensor shapes and static memory allocations, which matches the repetitive token-by-token decode loop but conflicts with dynamic, variable-length prefill prompts
CUDA Graphs only support integer quantization kernels and cannot record floating-point matrix multiplications used during prefill
CUDA Graphs execute exclusively on CPU cores and cannot capture GPU kernels that exceed 1000 TFLOP/s
CUDA Graphs require disaggregated serving network fabrics to replay kernel dispatches across multiple nodes
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Stable captured work lets graph replay reduce repeated host launch overhead. Decode often admits such a repetitive execution region, while varying prefill shapes require bucketing, padding, updates, or separate captures. Capture also depends on memory-address and operation constraints; variable prompts do not make graph use universally impossible. Integer-only or CPU-only execution is not the explanation.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the operational constraints and execution prerequisites of CUDA Graphs in LLM serving pipelines

questions.question: FlashAttention performs strictly MORE total floating-point operations (FLOPs) than standard unfused attention due to online softmax rescaling. Explain the systems principle that allows FlashAttention to achieve a 2–4$\times$ wall-clock speedup despite executing more arithmetic.
questions.answer: Standard unfused attention materializes score and probability matrices in HBM. FlashAttention tiles the computation so these intermediates remain on chip. Extra rescaling arithmetic can be cheaper than the removed HBM traffic when data movement is the bottleneck. The additional work is not literally free or necessarily executed on Tensor Cores; the net gain depends on sequence length, kernel implementation, and the resulting resource limits.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the I/O-aware systems trade-off of trading extra arithmetic operations in SRAM to eliminate off-chip HBM traffic

questions.question: True or False: Wrapping an unfused PyTorch layer in a CUDA Graph automatically fuses adjacent element-wise kernels into a single GPU kernel to eliminate intermediate high-bandwidth memory (HBM) writes.
questions.answer: False. CUDA Graphs only eliminate CPU-side launch latency and dispatch overhead by recording and replaying a static graph of kernel launches in a single CPU command. CUDA Graphs do not inspect, rewrite, or fuse GPU kernel code; eliminating intermediate HBM writes requires operator fusion via compilers (like `torch.compile` / TorchInductor) or custom hand-written Triton/CUDA kernels.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish between launch-overhead elimination via CUDA Graphs and memory-traffic reduction via operator fusion

questions.question: Consider a bias-GELU-dropout chain applied to a tensor with hidden dimension 4096 and batch size 2048 in FP16. The unfused path launches three kernels and materializes two intermediate tensors of approximately 16.8 MB each. If a fused kernel can retain their values in registers or SRAM, how does fusion change memory traffic and execution?
choices: It increases total HBM traffic to 128 MB because the fused kernel must write debug checkpoints after each sub-operation
It removes four intermediate transfers totaling approximately 67.1 MB and reduces three launches to one, while preserving the input read and final output write
It converts the operation into a pure CPU task to bypass GPU shared memory allocation limits
It eliminates the need to load the weight matrix $W$ from HBM by synthesizing weights dynamically in registers
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Each of two intermediates contains 2048 × 4096 × 2 bytes, or about 16.8 MB. Writing and rereading both costs four such transfers, about 67.1 MB (64 MiB). Fusion removes those transfers when the intermediate values remain on chip. It does not eliminate required input reads or create model weights; register pressure and occupancy still constrain the implementation.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate intermediate memory traffic savings and launch overhead reduction achieved through operator fusion

focus_areas: Outlier features in LLMs and mitigation strategies (LLM.int8, AWQ, SmoothQuant)
Block-wise quantization metadata trade-offs
PTQ calibration vs QAT training-time costs
Weight-only vs weight-activation quantization regimes and KV cache precision dividends
rationale.question_strategy: Compare outlier mitigation strategies in an MCQ, contrast weight-only vs weight-activation regimes in a SHORT question, evaluate block-wise quantization metadata scaling in a TF question, and analyze the batch-capacity precision dividend in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Outlier mechanism comparison -> operational regime trade-offs -> metadata scaling analysis -> multi-GPU capacity synthesis.
rationale.integration: Links numerical representations to hardware throughput and serving memory capacity.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Crucial precision engineering section balancing numerical fidelity, memory bandwidth, and batch capacity.

questions.question: Large Language Models exhibit emergent activation outlier features where $\sim 0.1\%$ of channels have magnitudes $3–20\times$ larger than normal. How does SmoothQuant enable efficient uniform INT8 quantization (W8A8) across both weights and activations without suffering catastrophic quality loss?
choices: SmoothQuant drops all outlier channels from the model entirely, using low-rank distillation to compensate for removed hidden dimensions
SmoothQuant splits the matrix multiplication at runtime into an FP16 branch for outliers and an INT8 branch for standard features

SmoothQuant applies a per-channel scaling factor that divides activations by $s$ and multiplies weights by $s$, migrating quantization difficulty from dynamic activations to static weights prior to inference
SmoothQuant computes an exact Hessian inverse across all layers during training using the straight-through estimator
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. SmoothQuant applies a per-channel scaling factor that divides activations by $s$ and multiplies weights by $s$, migrating quantization difficulty from dynamic activations to static weights prior to inference. Because activation outliers are concentrated in specific channels across all tokens, multiplying the weights by the per-channel scale and dividing the inputs by the same scale is mathematically equivalent. This smooths activation peaks at the cost of slightly increasing weight dynamic range, enabling uniform INT8 quantization on both weights and activations (W8A8) to leverage INT8 Tensor Cores. The runtime branch approach describes LLM.int8(), the Hessian inverse refers to GPTQ, and dropping channels is a destructive heuristic.
questions.learning_objective: Compare mathematical strategies for mitigating activation outlier channels during low-bit quantization

questions.question: Contrast weight-only quantization (e.g. AWQ INT4) with weight-activation quantization (e.g. SmoothQuant W8A8 or FP8) in terms of target serving operational regime (batch size) and hardware execution units used.
questions.answer: Weight-only INT4 quantization targets memory-bound inference at small batch sizes (e.g. batch size 1 decode), where the primary bottleneck is streaming weights from HBM; weights are dequantized on-the-fly to FP16 and executed on standard FP16 Tensor Cores. Weight-activation quantization (W8A8 or FP8) quantizes both operands, targeting compute-bound inference at large batch sizes or training, executing directly on INT8 or FP8 Tensor Cores to double arithmetic compute throughput in addition to reducing memory traffic.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the operational trade-offs and hardware utilization differences between weight-only and weight-activation quantization

questions.question: True or False: In block-wise INT4 quantization, reducing the group block size $G_{\text{block}}$ from 64 to 16 reduces quantization error but quadruples the scale-factor metadata overhead from 0.25 bits/weight (6.25% overhead on INT4) to 1.0 bit/weight (25% overhead on INT4).
questions.answer: True. With block-wise quantization, each group of $G_{\text{block}}$ weights shares one 16-bit FP16 scale factor. For $G_{\text{block}} = 64$, the scale adds $16/64 = 0.25$ bits per weight (a $0.25/4 = 6.25\%$ overhead relative to 4-bit payload). For $G_{\text{block}} = 16$, the scale adds $16/16 = 1.0$ bit per weight (a $1.0/4 = 25\%$ overhead relative to 4-bit payload), yielding an effective bit-width of 5.0 bits/weight.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the metadata overhead and effective bit-width scaling of block-wise quantization group sizes

questions.question: A 70B model uses 17.5 GB of weights per GPU on eight 80 GB GPUs. Ignoring runtime reserves and quantization metadata, INT4 weights use approximately 4.4 GB per GPU and INT8 KV cache halves the per-token cache footprint. Why does the KV capacity gain combine two distinct effects rather than equal the fourfold weight reduction?
choices: Because INT4 weights bypass the GPU memory hierarchy and execute directly from CPU system RAM
Because quantizing the KV cache converts autoregressive decoding into non-autoregressive parallel generation
Because INT8 KV cache pages eliminate the need for GPU virtual address translation tables in PagedAttention

Because reducing weights from 17.5 GB to 4.4 GB expands available KV cache space from 62.5 GB to 75.6 GB per GPU, which—when multiplied by halving the per-request INT8 KV cache footprint—multiplicatively expands total admitted batch capacity
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The ideal KV budget grows from 62.5 GB to 75.6 GB, a factor of 75.6/62.5 ≈ 1.21. Halving bytes per cached token multiplies capacity by another two, yielding approximately 2.42 times the original token capacity, not more than four times. Runtime reserves, metadata, sequence lengths, and scheduler policy reduce the deployable batch limit; quantization does not remove autoregressive dependencies or page tables.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize how weight and KV-cache quantization interact multiplicatively to expand serving batch capacity

rationale.question_strategy: Order the stages of the compilation pipeline, examine TorchDynamo bytecode interception and graph breaks, calculate compilation speedup dividends in a SHORT question, test compiler mode terminology in a FILL question, and contrast XLA whole-program compilation with PyTorch.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Pipeline sequencing -> bytecode mechanism analysis -> worked speedup calculation -> terminology recall -> compiler paradigm comparison.
rationale.integration: Explains how modern compiler stacks automate fusion and memory planning across diverse accelerator architectures.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Essential systems section on compiler technology and automated optimization frameworks.

questions.question:
Arrange the following stages of the deep learning graph compilation pipeline in their standard logical order of execution:

(1) Operator Fusion Pass (identifying fusible subgraphs to eliminate intermediate HBM round-trips)
(2) Graph Capture (tracing Python code to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph of tensor operations)
(3) Kernel Selection and Code Generation (generating and autotuning backend Triton/CUDA machine code)
(4) Memory Planning Pass (analyzing tensor lifetimes and scheduling physical buffer reuse)
(5) Graph-Level Optimization (applying algebraic simplifications and constant folding)
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) Graph Capture -> (5) Graph-Level Optimization -> (1) Operator Fusion Pass -> (4) Memory Planning Pass -> (3) Kernel Selection and Code Generation. The compiler first captures the computation into a DAG, performs device-agnostic algebraic simplifications, identifies adjacent operations to fuse, plans memory allocations across the simplified and fused graph, and finally lowers the optimized subgraphs into specialized machine code.
questions.learning_objective: Order the core transformation stages of a deep learning graph compilation pipeline

questions.question: How does TorchDynamo in PyTorch 2.0 capture computation graphs from standard Python code, and what is the systems impact when it encounters an unsupported dynamic construct (such as data-dependent Python control flow)?
choices: TorchDynamo intercepts CPython frame evaluation at the bytecode level (via PEP 523); when encountering untraceable Python constructs, it inserts a Graph Break that splits the trace into separate subgraphs, preventing fusion across the break boundary
TorchDynamo compiles Python source text into static C++ before execution; when encountering dynamic control flow, it aborts the process with a fatal runtime exception
TorchDynamo executes an abstract syntax tree rewriter that replaces all Python loops with CUDA thread blocks, ignoring data-dependent conditions
TorchDynamo runs exclusively ahead-of-time, forcing all dynamic variables to fixed constants during model export
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. TorchDynamo intercepts CPython frame evaluation at the bytecode level (via PEP 523); when encountering untraceable Python constructs, it inserts a Graph Break that splits the trace into separate subgraphs, preventing fusion across the break boundary. By hooking frame evaluation at the bytecode interpreter level, TorchDynamo captures graphs without requiring model code modifications. However, graph breaks divide execution into smaller compiled fragments separated by Python interpreter overhead, reducing the scope for cross-operator fusion and memory planning. The other choices incorrectly describe fatal exceptions, AST loop rewriting, or forced ahead-of-time constant evaluation.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the bytecode interception mechanism of TorchDynamo and analyze the performance impact of graph breaks

questions.question: A 13B model in PyTorch eager mode spends 50% of step time in GEMMs (4.17 ms), 35% in element-wise operations (2.92 ms), and 15% in kernel launch overhead (1.25 ms), totaling 8.33 ms per token (120 tokens/s). Applying `torch.compile` eliminates 80% of launch overhead and reduces element-wise time by 70% via fusion while leaving GEMM time unchanged. Calculate the new step time, the resulting throughput, and identify the new dominant bottleneck.
questions.answer: New GEMM time = 4.17 ms. New element-wise time = $2.92 \times (1 - 0.70) = 0.88\text{ ms}$. New launch overhead = $1.25 \times (1 - 0.80) = 0.25\text{ ms}$. New total step time = $4.17 + 0.88 + 0.25 = 5.30\text{ ms}$, yielding a throughput of $1000 / 5.30 \approx 189\text{ tokens/s}$ (a $1.58\times$ speedup). The new dominant bottleneck is the GEMM computation itself, which now accounts for $4.17 / 5.30 \approx 79\%$ of total step time.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the quantitative throughput speedup and identify the new dominant bottleneck resulting from compiler fusion and launch overhead reduction

questions.question: In `torch.compile`, the compilation mode that exhaustively benchmarks multiple candidate tile sizes, thread block configurations, and memory access patterns on the target GPU to select the fastest implementation is called ____.
questions.answer: max-autotune. This mode benchmarks candidate implementations and retains a fast choice for the target workload and hardware, trading compilation work for subsequent execution efficiency.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the torch.compile configuration mode responsible for hardware kernel autotuning

questions.question: How does XLA's whole-program compilation model (used in JAX/TPU workflows) differ fundamentally from PyTorch's `torch.compile` TorchDynamo tracing approach, and what is the primary operational trade-off?
choices: XLA generates Python bytecode on every forward pass, trading compilation speed for execution latency

XLA enforces a static whole-program graph, enabling global cross-layer optimizations and automated GSPMD distributed sharding at the cost of multi-minute compilation times and shape-change recompilations
XLA executes only on CPU hosts, whereas TorchDynamo compiles directly to TPU hardware
XLA requires dynamic shapes and cannot optimize static tensor dimensions
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. XLA enforces a static whole-program graph, enabling global cross-layer optimizations and automated GSPMD distributed sharding at the cost of multi-minute compilation times and shape-change recompilations. XLA treats the entire program as a static DAG, enabling systolic array dimension padding ($128 \times 128$ TPU units) and automatic collective insertion (GSPMD), achieving 55–65% MFU on production training. However, any change in batch size or sequence length triggers expensive recompilations. TorchDynamo prioritizes dynamic Python agility, using bytecode interception and graph breaks to compile subgraphs with minimal startup latency. The other options state false claims about CPU execution or dynamic shape requirements.
questions.learning_objective: Compare whole-program static compilation in XLA with incremental bytecode tracing in TorchDynamo

focus_areas: Speculative decoding mechanics, acceptance math, and roofline shifts
Correctness guarantees via residual resampling
Batching limits and diminishing returns of speculation
Mixture of Experts sparse routing, AllToAll communication, and load imbalance
rationale.question_strategy: Probe speculative decoding correctness guarantees and roofline impact in an MCQ, explain batch-size sensitivity in a SHORT question, address MoE scaling misconceptions in a TF question, and evaluate effective ITL speedup in a scenario MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Distributional correctness -> batch dynamics analysis -> distributed MoE trade-offs -> quantitative latency calculation.
rationale.integration: Shows how algorithmic restructuring changes the work term $O$ in the iron law while preserving model output contracts.
rationale.ranking_explanation: High-leverage section introducing algorithmic modifications that move the roofline operating point.

questions.question: Why does speculative decoding accelerate autoregressive generation on modern GPUs without altering the target model's output probability distribution?
choices: It forces the draft model to use the exact same weights as the target model through FP8 weight quantizing
It skips attention computation for all tokens where the draft model confidence exceeds 50%

It accepts candidate draft tokens with probability $\min(1, p_\theta / q_\phi)$ and resamples rejected tokens from the positive residual $(p_\theta - q_\phi)_+$, ensuring strict mathematical equivalence while verifying $K$ tokens in a single parallel target pass to amortize weight-streaming bandwidth
It runs the draft model and target model on separate GPUs connected via PCIe, bypassing HBM bandwidth limits entirely
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. It accepts candidate draft tokens with probability $\min(1, p_\theta / q_\phi)$ and resamples rejected tokens from the positive residual $(p_\theta - q_\phi)_+$, ensuring strict mathematical equivalence while verifying $K$ tokens in a single parallel target pass to amortize weight-streaming bandwidth. In memory-bound decode, loading target model weights from HBM once can verify $K$ candidate tokens simultaneously in a single compute pass ($[K, d_{\text{model}}] \times [d_{\text{model}}, d_{\text{model}}]$), effectively shifting the arithmetic intensity $K\times$ rightward toward the roofline ridge. The acceptance-rejection math guarantees that the emitted token sequence matches the target model distribution $p_\theta$ exactly. The other choices describe non-existent confidence thresholds, weight quantization confusion, or PCIe offloading.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how speculative decoding achieves latency speedups while preserving exact target model output distributions

questions.question: Explain why speculative decoding provides substantial speedup at batch size 1 but exhibits diminishing or even negative returns as serving batch size increases (e.g. batch size 64).
questions.answer: At small batches, target verification can reuse one weight pass across several candidate positions while arithmetic units have spare capacity. Larger batches already amortize weight reads, so additional verification and draft work can erase that benefit. The crossover is workload-dependent: batch size 64 alone does not establish compute saturation. Measure accepted output per round, draft and verification costs, and loaded throughput before enabling speculation.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the interaction between speculative decoding efficiency and serving batch size dynamics

questions.question: True or False: In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, scaling the number of experts from 8 to 256 is a cost-free capacity scaling knob because each token only activates top-$k$ experts during inference.
questions.answer: False. More experts increase total weight capacity even when each token activates a fixed number. Distributing them can add communication, routing imbalance, and latency, but transferred activation bytes do not necessarily grow with total expert count when token count, top-k, and representation size are fixed. Placement and the number of destinations determine the actual network cost.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the system-level memory, communication, and load balancing costs of scaling expert counts in MoE models

questions.question: In a speculative decoding deployment, draft generation takes 4 ms and target verification takes 32 ms. Measurements show a mean of 3.5 emitted tokens per round, including correction or bonus tokens. What is the amortized time per emitted token and speedup over a 32 ms autoregressive baseline?
choices: Effective ITL is 36.0 ms/token, representing a $0.89\times$ slowdown due to draft model overhead
Effective ITL is 7.2 ms/token, representing a $4.4\times$ speedup
Effective ITL is 20.5 ms/token, representing a $1.56\times$ speedup
Approximately 10.3 ms per emitted token and a 3.1-fold amortized speedup
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A round takes 4 + 32 = 36 ms and emits 3.5 tokens on average, so amortized time is 36/3.5 ≈ 10.29 ms per token and speedup is 32/10.29 ≈ 3.11. Dividing by all five candidate tokens would wrongly assume full acceptance. This average does not establish an inter-token latency percentile because outputs can arrive in blocks.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate amortized time per emitted token from measured round cost and output yield.

focus_areas: Exposed-time test and overlap condition ($T_{\text{comm}} \leq T_{\text{compute}}$)
CUDA streams, asynchronous execution, and event synchronization
Physical SM partitioning and interference penalties
DDP bucket backward hooks and multi-node scaling degradation
rationale.question_strategy: Formulate the exposed-time overlap condition in an MCQ, analyze SM partitioning penalties in a SHORT question, order the sequence of DDP gradient overlap, and verify multi-stream synchronization hazards in a TF question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Mathematical condition check -> physical hardware contention -> runtime execution ordering -> synchronization hazard analysis.
rationale.integration: Connects single-device execution with multi-GPU distributed collectives, grounding communication hiding in CUDA stream mechanics.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core distributed performance engineering section addressing inter-device communication bottlenecks.

questions.question: Under the exposed-time formulation of communication-computation overlap ($T_{\text{step}} = \max(T_{\text{compute}}, T_{\text{comm}}) + T_{\text{sync}}$), what physical condition is required to achieve 100% communication hiding (zero exposed communication time)?
choices: $T_{\text{comm}} \leq T_{\text{compute}}$, meaning the network data transfer duration is fully bounded within the concurrent local GPU compute window
$T_{\text{comm}} = 0$, requiring all distributed GPUs to share a single physical HBM memory controller
$T_{\text{compute}} = 0$, requiring the GPU to execute collective operations without running backward pass gradients
$T_{\text{comm}} \ge 2 \times T_{\text{compute}}$, ensuring communication has priority over SM scheduling
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. $T_{\text{comm}} \leq T_{\text{compute}}$, meaning the network data transfer duration is fully bounded within the concurrent local GPU compute window. Overlap removes communication from the critical path only when local computation takes longer than the concurrent network collective ($T_{\text{comm}} - T_{\text{overlap}} \le 0$). When $T_{\text{comm}} > T_{\text{compute}}$ (as often occurs across slow inter-node Ethernet or when scaling to 1024 GPUs), the excess communication $(T_{\text{comm}} - T_{\text{compute}})$ remains exposed and stalls the step. The other choices describe physically impossible zero-time assumptions or inverted conditions.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the exposed-time test to determine whether inter-device communication is fully hidden behind concurrent computation

questions.question: Describe the physical mechanism of 'SM Partitioning' when running concurrent compute and NCCL communication streams on an accelerator like the NVIDIA H100, and explain why a 3–6% compute throughput penalty is considered an acceptable trade-off.
questions.answer: Some communication implementations use SM resources that would otherwise execute GEMMs. Reserving resources can therefore reduce local compute throughput while allowing collective transfers to overlap useful computation. A few percent compute penalty is worthwhile only if the reduction in exposed communication is larger; SM counts and the benefit depend on the collective, transport, hardware, and workload rather than a fixed universal reservation.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the physical resource contention mechanism of SM partitioning during concurrent compute and communication execution

questions.question:
In PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP), arrange the following events in the exact sequence that implements asynchronous gradient communication overlap during training:

(1) Main compute stream continues backward pass execution on earlier layers concurrently with network transfer
(2) Autograd backward pass computes parameter gradients for a layer
(3) Event barrier synchronizes the communication stream with the compute stream before optimizer step
(4) Autograd backward hook triggers asynchronous AllReduce on the parameter bucket in a dedicated NCCL stream
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) Autograd backward pass computes parameter gradients for a layer -> (4) Autograd backward hook triggers asynchronous AllReduce on the parameter bucket in a dedicated NCCL stream -> (1) Main compute stream continues backward pass execution on earlier layers concurrently with network transfer -> (3) Event barrier synchronizes the communication stream with the compute stream before optimizer step. As gradients are computed, hooks dispatch non-blocking AllReduces on a side stream while backward propagation continues on the main stream, synchronizing only at the end of the backward pass.
questions.learning_objective: Order the runtime sequence of PyTorch DDP bucketed gradient communication and backward computation overlap

questions.question: True or False: In multi-stream CUDA programming, launching an asynchronous memory copy or NCCL collective on a side stream without explicit `event.record()` and `event.wait()` synchronization against the default stream can cause silent data corruption because the collective may read tensors before the producing kernel finishes writing them.
questions.answer: True. CUDA streams execute sequentially internally, but operations across different streams execute concurrently without implicit order. If a kernel on Stream A writes a tensor and Stream B launches an AllReduce reading that tensor without an explicit `cudaEventRecord` on Stream A and `cudaStreamWaitEvent` on Stream B, the GPU hardware scheduler may execute the read before the write completes, causing silent data races.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze multi-stream CUDA synchronization hazards and data race conditions

focus_areas: The Heisenberg effect of profiling and allocator interference
4-level profiling hierarchy (Application to Hardware Counters)
MFU vs MBU metric selection for training vs decode
Nsight Systems timeline pattern recognition (CUDA HW, CUDA API, NCCL, NVTX)
Tensor Core alignment and silent fallback to CUDA Cores
rationale.question_strategy: Contrast MFU vs MBU for decode inference in an MCQ, outline the 4-level diagnostic sequence in a SHORT question, test Tensor Core alignment terminology in a FILL question, examine profiler memory inflation in an MCQ, and correct CUDA API timeline misconceptions in a TF question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Metric disambiguation -> diagnostic protocol synthesis -> hardware counter recall -> observer effect analysis -> timeline pattern evaluation.
rationale.integration: Provides the empirical diagnostic framework required to identify bottlenecks across all system layers.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Foundational methodology section teaching systematic measurement over intuitive guesswork.

questions.question: A production LLM serving decode step on an NVIDIA H100 reports a Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) of only 2.5%, but a Model Bandwidth Utilization (MBU) of 86%. How should the performance engineer interpret these diagnostic metrics?
choices: The GPU hardware is malfunctioning and must be power-cycled to clear thermal throttling
The measurements are consistent with a bandwidth-limited path; low MFU alone is not evidence of poor implementation when MBU is high
The low MFU indicates severe kernel launch latency on the CPU dispatcher that requires rewriting into CUDA Graphs
The high MBU indicates excessive gradient checkpointing overhead that is saturating the PCIe bus
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. High MBU and low MFU can be consistent with a memory-bound decode path rather than defective hardware or dominant launch gaps. Check FLOPs and bytes at the same boundary: 2.5% of 989 TFLOP/s divided by 86% of 3.35 TB/s implies about 8.6 FLOP/byte, not one. Further diagnosis should test redundant traffic and the request critical path before declaring the entire service optimal.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the diagnostic roles of Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) and Model Bandwidth Utilization (MBU) across training and inference regimes

questions.question: Using the 4-level profiling hierarchy (Application, Distributed/Communication, Trace/Timeline, Operation/Hardware Counters), describe the step-by-step drill-down sequence an engineer should use to diagnose an LLM serving pipeline that misses its P99 latency SLA.
questions.answer: Start with application metrics such as P99 first-token and inter-token latency. Use framework traces across ranks to localize scheduling, data-transfer, or collective delays. Inspect kernel timelines to distinguish launch gaps, late arrival, and serialized work. Finally, use hardware counters on the implicated kernel to test memory bandwidth, occupancy, and instruction mix. Distributed scope cuts across this application-to-hardware hierarchy; it is not a separate fixed level.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize a structured multi-level profiling diagnostic protocol to isolate performance bottlenecks

questions.question: If profiling confirms that a matrix operation uses scalar GPU arithmetic rather than Tensor Core instructions, the scalar units are called ____ Cores; tensor dimensions alone do not establish that execution path.
questions.answer: CUDA. Kernel selection depends on datatype, shape, library, and hardware. Misalignment may reduce efficiency without universally forcing a scalar fallback; inspect the executed instruction mix.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish scalar CUDA execution from Tensor Core execution using profiling evidence.

questions.question: Why can enabling shape recording in a high-fidelity PyTorch profiler perturb tensor lifetimes and increase memory demand in a workload that runs stably without profiling?
choices: The profiler increases GPU clock frequency beyond thermal limits, triggering emergency memory shutdowns
The profiler converts all FP16 tensors to FP64 double-precision matrices during recording
Shape recording can retain tensor references, inhibit reference-count-dependent optimizations, and introduce extra copies
The profiler overwrites the CUDA driver's virtual memory page tables with TensorBoard logs
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Shape recording can retain tensor references and affect optimizations or copies, so the instrumented run may require more memory. Allocation-history recording instead records allocator events and has metadata overhead; it should not be assumed to keep every activation alive. Compare matched instrumented and uninstrumented runs rather than attributing the change to clock rates or automatic precision conversion.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the observer effect (Heisenberg effect) of profiling tools on memory allocation and system behavior

questions.question: True or False: In an NVIDIA Nsight Systems trace, observing that the CUDA API row on the CPU thread displays wide bars significantly larger than the corresponding CUDA HW kernel bars indicates that the GPU kernels are executing too slowly.
questions.answer: False. Wide CPU API bars do not show that GPU kernels themselves are slow. They may reflect host launch overhead, synchronization, or blocking calls. Correlate them with GPU idle gaps and dependencies before diagnosing a host-submission bottleneck; graph replay helps only the overhead it actually removes.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate CPU-GPU interaction patterns and launch bottlenecks on Nsight Systems timeline traces

focus_areas: Fleet MFU vs Local MFU and the Scaling Tax
Small-scale canaries, fleet baselines, and gray failure detection
Straggler amplification in synchronous distributed systems
Hero run tax: MLPerf benchmarks vs production realities
rationale.question_strategy: Calculate the Scaling Tax across a 128-GPU cluster in an MCQ, explain straggler amplification from a single gray failure node in a SHORT question, test benchmark terminology in a FILL question, and evaluate regression testing tiers in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Quantitative scaling tax calculation -> distributed straggler mechanics -> terminology recall -> regression testing strategy.
rationale.integration: Scales node-level profiling to thousands of accelerators, addressing network jitter, multi-node stragglers, and fleet telemetry.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Crucial section bridging single-node engineering to fleet-scale distributed infrastructure.

questions.question: A 70B parameter model achieves 65% MFU on an isolated 8-GPU node. When scaled across a 128-GPU cluster connected via InfiniBand, the training step time increases such that cluster-wide MFU drops to 48%. What is the Scaling Tax incurred by this distributed deployment?
choices: 17.0% Scaling Tax, calculated as the direct difference ($65\% - 48\%$)
35.4% Scaling Tax, calculated as the ratio of unutilized compute ($1 - 0.48 / 0.65$)
52.0% Scaling Tax, representing the unutilized fraction of the 128 GPUs

Approximately 26.2% Scaling Tax ($1 - \text{Fleet MFU} / \text{Local MFU} = 1 - 0.48 / 0.65$), representing the fraction of single-node efficiency lost to inter-node communication and barrier synchronization
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Approximately 26.2% Scaling Tax ($1 - \text{Fleet MFU} / \text{Local MFU} = 1 - 0.48 / 0.65$), representing the fraction of single-node efficiency lost to inter-node communication and barrier synchronization. The Scaling Tax measures the relative loss of efficiency when transitioning from a local node baseline to multi-node scale: $\text{Scaling Tax} = 1 - (\text{MFU}_{\text{fleet}} / \text{MFU}_{\text{local}}) = 1 - (0.48 / 0.65) = 1 - 0.7385 \approx 26.2\%$. Reporting raw percentage-point differences ($65\% - 48\% = 17\%$) confuses absolute percentage points with relative scaling efficiency loss.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate and interpret the distributed Scaling Tax from single-node and fleet-wide MFU metrics

questions.question: In a synchronous data-parallel cluster of 1,000 GPUs, explain why one gray-failure node that delivers 10% less processing throughput can reduce the entire fleet's useful throughput by roughly 10% when its work determines every step's critical path.
questions.answer: All ranks must complete their required work before a synchronized step can advance. A rank delivering 90% of normal throughput takes 1/0.9 ≈ 1.111 times as long for the same work, so the fleet can be limited to 90% of its original throughput. The result assumes that this delay is exposed and dominates the critical path. A 10% increase in duration would instead imply about a 9.1% throughput loss.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how barrier synchronization amplifies single-node gray failures and stragglers into cluster-wide throughput collapses

questions.question: The 10–20% throughput gap between highly tuned, unmonitored benchmark configurations (such as MLPerf) and real-world production clusters burdened by checkpointing, health heartbeats, logging, and thermal entropy is known as the ____ run tax.
questions.answer: hero. Benchmark configurations can exclude production duties such as checkpointing and monitoring. Capacity planning must measure that gap under the actual operating workload rather than assume a fixed percentage.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the industry term describing the efficiency gap between idealized benchmark runs and production deployments

questions.question: Which tiered testing strategy is specifically designed to catch nonlinear scaling collapses (such as exhausted InfiniBand credit buffers or garbage collection pauses) before deploying a code change to a 1,000-GPU cluster?
choices: Small-scale canaries on 8 and 64 GPUs to map the scaling efficiency curve and identify curve-bending regressions before full-fleet deployment
Single-GPU unit tests running with Python debug assertions enabled
Synthetic micro-benchmarks that test only CPU RAM bandwidth
Static code linting to count the number of matrix multiplications in the model
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Small-scale canaries on 8 and 64 GPUs to map the scaling efficiency curve and identify curve-bending regressions before full-fleet deployment. Scaling regressions are inherently distributed and nonlinear; changes that introduce negligible overhead on 1 GPU can trigger severe network buffer exhaustion or synchronization stalls at scale. Testing on intermediate multi-node canaries (8 and 64 GPUs) maps the scaling slope, catching efficiency anomalies before committing full-fleet resources. Single-GPU tests, static linters, and CPU micro-benchmarks cannot observe distributed collective and interconnect behaviors.
questions.learning_objective: Design a tiered regression testing protocol to detect distributed scaling anomalies prior to full-fleet deployment

sections.section_title: Optimization Playbook for Large Language Models

focus_areas: Diagnostic sequencing: Precision -> Fusion -> Speculation
Bottleneck displacement across optimization rounds
Compounding effects of INT4 weights, INT8 KV cache, FlashAttention-2, and CUDA Graphs
Adaptive speculative decoding policy under varying load
rationale.question_strategy: Order the optimization rounds in the 70B case study, explain why precision engineering precedes fusion and speculation in an MCQ, analyze adaptive speculation batch thresholds in a SHORT question, and diagnose intermediate bottleneck displacement in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Optimization round sequencing -> architectural dependency reasoning -> load-dependent policy analysis -> bottleneck displacement diagnosis.
rationale.integration: Synthesizes all individual techniques into a cohesive, production-grade optimization case study on a 70B model.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Capstone case study section showing how disparate optimizations compound sequentially.

questions.question: In the constructed batch-one 70B decode budget, order the three optimization experiments: (1) Operator fusion and graph replay, (2) Weight precision reduction, (3) Speculative decoding.
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) Weight precision reduction -> (1) Operator fusion and graph replay -> (3) Speculative decoding. Precision first reduces the exposed GEMM interval. Fusion and replay then reduce attention, element-wise, and launch intervals. Speculation finally changes output per target pass. Each round uses explicit assumptions and a shared timing boundary; the sequence is not a universal optimization order.
questions.learning_objective: Order the experiments in a constructed decode budget and explain their shared accounting boundary.

questions.question: Why does the constructed batch-one 70B decode example test INT4 weights before speculative decoding or operator fusion?
choices: Because the GPU driver disables CUDA Graphs and compiler optimizations unless weights are formatted in INT4
The assumed profile identifies weight traffic as the first target; reducing its exposed GEMM interval provides a consistent baseline for subsequent experiments
Because speculative decoding cannot mathematically operate on FP16 models
Because operator fusion only works on models with fewer than 10 billion parameters
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The example assumes weight streaming is the first target and tests a 45% reduction in its exposed GEMM interval while leaving other intervals unchanged. It does not infer a batch expansion or simultaneous throughput gain from freed memory. Compiler restrictions, model-size limits, and an inability to speculate in FP16 are not the reason for this order.
questions.learning_objective: Justify the architectural sequencing of optimization interventions in a production LLM serving pipeline

questions.question: Why must a serving controller measure the batch-size crossover for speculative decoding rather than infer a universal cutoff from a batch-one decode budget?
questions.answer: Batching already shares weight reads across requests, reducing the spare compute that makes verification economical. Draft overhead, acceptance, cache capacity, and verification kernels determine where speculation stops improving useful service. The batch-one budget establishes no cutoff at 16 or any other batch size. Measure latency and loaded throughput for the draft-target pair under the intended request mix before selecting a policy.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the systems rationale for load-dependent adaptive speculative decoding policies

questions.question: An 85 ms decode step has exposed intervals of 32.3 ms GEMM, 20.4 ms attention, 11.9 ms element-wise work, 10.2 ms AllReduce, and 10.2 ms launch/runtime overhead. Reducing only GEMM time by 45% leaves 70.465 ms. Why does this still miss a 50 ms objective?
choices: The InfiniBand network cable was disconnected during the benchmark run
The GPU ran out of power and throttled clock frequency to zero
The unchanged non-GEMM intervals still total 52.7 ms, so reducing GEMM alone by the assumed amount cannot reach the objective
INT4 quantization caused the model to produce infinite repetitive token loops
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. GEMM becomes 32.3 × 0.55 = 17.765 ms, while all other exposed intervals remain 52.7 ms; the sum is 70.465 ms. The next experiment must address other critical-path costs. With attention at 14.28 ms, element-wise work at 3.4 ms, and launch/runtime overhead at 2 ms, the later constructed budget totals 47.645 ms; these are assumptions, not benchmark claims.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze bottleneck displacement across iterative optimization rounds using timeline breakdown data

focus_areas: Peak FLOP/s vs memory bandwidth for inference
FP8 adoption vs communication/launch overheads
The long tail of small kernels vs GEMM optimization
Speculative decoding under batching
MoE expert scaling limits
Average latency vs tail latency protection
rationale.question_strategy: Expose the peak FLOP/s inference fallacy in an MCQ, analyze tail latency vs average latency protection in a SHORT question, evaluate FP8 training halving claims in a TF question, and address compiler limits vs algorithmic innovations in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Inference hardware fallacy -> tail latency systems diagnostics -> precision scaling nuance -> compiler boundary evaluation.
rationale.integration: Directly counters pervasive engineering misconceptions regarding hardware specs, compilers, and scaling knobs.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Critical synthesis section exposing common architectural traps and operational failures.

questions.question: A team upgrades their LLM serving cluster from NVIDIA A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a $3\times$ reduction in generation latency based on the H100's $3\times$ higher peak FP16 TFLOP/s rating. However, batch-1 autoregressive decode latency improves by only ~15%. What fundamental performance engineering fallacy explains this result?
choices: The fallacy that H100 GPUs cannot execute FP16 operations without INT4 emulation
The fallacy that Python cannot run on Hopper-architecture accelerators
The fallacy that PyTorch profiler traces disable GPU Tensor Cores during inference

The fallacy that raw compute capacity dictates inference speed: batch-1 decode is bound by HBM memory bandwidth (~1 FLOP/byte), so doubling compute FLOP/s yields negligible speedup when memory bandwidth grows much more modestly
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The fallacy that raw compute capacity dictates inference speed: batch-1 decode is bound by HBM memory bandwidth (~1 FLOP/byte), so doubling compute FLOP/s yields negligible speedup when memory bandwidth grows much more modestly. Roofline analysis shows that batch-1 decode operates deep in the memory-bound regime. An H100 offers $\sim 3.35\text{ TB/s}$ bandwidth compared to A100's $\sim 2.0\text{ TB/s}$ ($1.67\times$ bandwidth increase), whereas compute increased $3.16\times$. Token generation rate is governed by how fast weights are read from memory ($D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$), not peak FLOP/s. Expecting compute ratings to dictate decode speed ignores the memory wall. The other choices present absurd claims about driver incompatibilities or disabled Tensor Cores.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the fallacy of using peak arithmetic FLOP/s ratings to project memory-bandwidth-bound inference performance

questions.question: Explain why evaluating LLM serving performance purely on average inter-token latency can mask severe production failures, and describe two specific systems engineering techniques used to optimize P99 tail latency.
questions.answer: Average latency can appear excellent (e.g. 30 ms) while users experience disruptive freezes due to high P99 latency (e.g. 500 ms) triggered by runtime garbage collection pauses, dynamic memory reallocation stalls, or network AllReduce jitter. Two systems techniques to protect P99 tail latency are: (1) preallocated static memory buffer pools (or PagedAttention blocks) to eliminate runtime dynamic allocation stalls, and (2) CUDA Graph replay, which eliminates variance in CPU kernel dispatch times.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the operational divergence between average latency and tail latency in serving systems and identify mitigation techniques

questions.question: True or False: Upgrading a distributed training workload from FP16 to FP8 precision automatically halves total step time across any multi-node GPU cluster.
questions.answer: False. Higher FP8 peak throughput applies to supported arithmetic, not automatically to the entire step. Uncompressed collectives, host dispatch, and unaffected kernels can remain unchanged, while lower precision may also reduce some memory traffic. End-to-end speedup depends on which exposed intervals change and whether model quality remains acceptable.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the limitations of low-precision arithmetic adoption under Amdahl's law in distributed training

questions.question: Why can automated deep learning graph compilers (like `torch.compile` or TensorRT) not automatically discover algorithmic transformations such as FlashAttention or Speculative Decoding?
choices: Graph compilers automate algebraic rewrites, memory planning, and fusion within a fixed mathematical computation graph; they cannot invent new mathematical formulations (like online softmax tiling) or new execution loops (like draft-verify speculative decoding)
Graph compilers are restricted by hardware law to only optimize CPU assembly code
Graph compilers only support models with fewer than 100,000 parameters
Graph compilers disable shared memory allocations on NVIDIA GPUs
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Graph compilers automate algebraic rewrites, memory planning, and fusion within a fixed mathematical computation graph; they cannot invent new mathematical formulations (like online softmax tiling) or new execution loops (like draft-verify speculative decoding). Compilers operate on known directed acyclic graphs, applying deterministic cost models to fuse adjacent operators and reuse buffers. FlashAttention required human mathematical insight to reformulate softmax into an incremental online algorithm that avoids quadratic memory, while speculative decoding altered the autoregressive execution loop. The other options make false claims about CPU restrictions, parameter limits, or shared memory disablement.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish between the automated optimization scope of graph compilers and the algorithmic innovations required of performance engineers

focus_areas: Three levers of the iron law ($D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$, $L_{\text{lat}}$, $O/R_{\text{peak}}$)
Optimization as continuous bottleneck displacement
Locality, precision, and algorithmic roofline movement
rationale.question_strategy: Order and match the three optimization pillars to their corresponding terms in the iron law, synthesize bottleneck displacement in a SHORT question, and evaluate the primacy of memory hierarchy optimization on modern accelerators in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Iron law mapping -> holistic methodology synthesis -> architectural primacy evaluation.
rationale.integration: Unifies the entire chapter's technical argument into the governing physical equation of ML performance.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Executive summary distilling the core principles of performance engineering.

questions.question:
Match and arrange the three primary performance engineering intervention pillars to the exact term of the iron law of ML performance ($T = D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}$) they directly optimize:

(1) Algorithmic Restructuring (Speculative Decoding, Mixture of Experts)
(2) Overhead & Latency Elimination (Graph Compilation, CUDA Graphs, Stream Overlap)
(3) Data Movement Reduction (Operator Fusion, FlashAttention, Precision Engineering)
questions.answer: The correct mapping and sequence is (3) Data Movement Reduction -> targets $D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$ (shrinking bytes transferred and eliminating HBM round-trips) -> (1) Algorithmic Restructuring -> targets $O / (R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}})$ (changing the fundamental operational work to verify multiple tokens or route sparsely) -> (2) Overhead & Latency Elimination -> targets $L_{\text{lat}}$ (eliminating CPU dispatch gaps, Python GIL overhead, and serialized communication).
questions.learning_objective: Map core performance engineering optimization pillars to the governing terms of the iron law of ML performance

questions.question: Summarize the concept of 'optimization as bottleneck displacement' (the waterbed problem) in performance engineering, and explain why continuous reprofiling is required after every optimization stage.
questions.answer: Accelerating the dominant bottleneck in an ML system does not produce infinite speedup; once that term shrinks, non-optimized secondary operations (such as launch overhead, memory-bound LayerNorms, or communication) become the new binding limit. Continuous reprofiling after each intervention is required to verify that the targeted bottleneck actually decreased, measure the newly exposed limiting factor, and ensure engineering effort is directed only at the active bottleneck.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize the principle of bottleneck displacement and justify the iterative profiling feedback loop

questions.question: On modern AI accelerators (such as the NVIDIA H100 with an FP16 ridge point of $\sim 295\text{ FLOP/byte}$ footed against 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth), why does performance engineering prioritize memory hierarchy optimizations (fusion, tiling, quantization) over raw compute throughput tuning for LLM inference?
choices: Because Tensor Cores are physically disabled during inference workloads

Because the vast majority of autoregressive inference operations have arithmetic intensities far below the ridge point (1–50 FLOP/byte), making execution time strictly bound by data movement across the memory hierarchy rather than arithmetic capacity
Because memory bandwidth is free and unlimited in modern cloud data centers
Because compiler graph optimizations only work on memory access instructions
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Because the vast majority of autoregressive inference operations have arithmetic intensities far below the ridge point (1–50 FLOP/byte), making execution time strictly bound by data movement across the memory hierarchy rather than arithmetic capacity. In generative LLM serving, token decoding streams gigabytes of weights and KV caches for a few arithmetic operations per element ($I \approx 1\text{ FLOP/byte}$). Under the roofline model, these operations sit deep on the sloped bandwidth ceiling, rendering peak compute throughput irrelevant until data movement is compressed through fusion, tiling (FlashAttention), and low-bit quantization. The other choices present absurd falsehoods about disabled hardware or unlimited bandwidth.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the architectural primacy of memory hierarchy optimization over compute throughput in modern accelerator workloads
